findings.title: Backup-code login path lets a caller skip password verification entirely
findings.body: Password verification only runs in the block at line 121 (`if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`), i.e. it is skipped whenever a non-empty `totpCode` is submitted. The new backup-code branch at line 131 (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)`) takes precedence over the TOTP branch, so a request that sends a dummy non-empty `totpCode` together with a valid `backupCode` has neither its password nor its TOTP code verified: the password check is skipped because `totpCode` is set, and the TOTP check is skipped because the backup-code branch ran instead. The result is that possession of a single backup code (e.g. from the downloaded `cal-backup-codes.txt`) is enough to sign in with just the e-mail address, downgrading 2FA from 'second factor' to 'only factor'. The branch should require that the password was actually verified (or verify it explicitly) before accepting a backup code.

findings.title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write
findings.body: The code decrypts `user.backupCodes`, nulls out the matched entry in memory and then writes the whole re-encrypted array back with `prisma.user.update`. Two requests that arrive concurrently both read the same pre-update array, so (a) the same backup code can be redeemed more than once (breaking the 'each code can be used exactly once' guarantee stated in `backup_code_instructions`), and (b) if two different codes are redeemed concurrently the second write resurrects the code invalidated by the first. Consuming the code needs to be atomic (e.g. a conditional/compare-and-set update inside a transaction, or storing codes in their own rows and deleting by unique key).

findings.title: Backup codes are matched case-sensitively and without trimming
findings.body: `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` only strips dashes. The generated codes are lowercase hex (`crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`), but users typically retype them from a printout and mobile keyboards auto-capitalise the first character, and copy/paste frequently adds surrounding whitespace. Any uppercase character or stray space makes a valid code be rejected with `IncorrectBackupCode`, consuming the user's rate-limit budget and potentially locking them out of the very recovery path this feature adds. Normalise with `.trim().toLowerCase()` (same issue exists in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` line 61).

findings.title: onEnable() is only invoked by the Close button, so dismissing the backup-code dialog leaves the parent UI stale
findings.body: Previously `onEnable()` was called as soon as the enable request succeeded (old line 135). Now success only advances to `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`, and `onEnable()` is called exclusively from the `backup-codes-close` button handler. If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (the Dialog's close/X control, Escape, clicking the overlay — all of which go through `onOpenChange`), 2FA is enabled server-side but the parent never runs its `onEnable` callback, so the two-factor switch / cached query is not refreshed and the settings page reports 2FA as disabled until a manual reload. `onEnable()` should also be fired when the dialog closes from the DisplayBackupCodes step.

findings.title: Submitting an empty backup code silently does nothing
findings.body: `BackupCode.tsx` relies on the HTML `required`/`minLength` attributes, but the login form is rendered with `noValidate` and the zod schema only validates `email`/`password` (`.passthrough()` for everything else), so an empty backup code is submitted. Server-side an empty `backupCode` is falsy, so the TOTP branch runs and returns `ErrorCode.SecondFactorRequired`, which this handler maps to `setTwoFactorRequired(true)` and shows no message at all. From the user's point of view pressing Submit on the 'Lost access' screen does nothing — no error, no feedback. Validate `backupCode` in the form schema (or map `SecondFactorRequired` to a visible error while in lost-access mode).

findings.title: Unvalidated request body can crash the disable endpoint
findings.body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` is called on whatever JSON the client sent. A non-string value (e.g. `{"backupCode": 1234567890}` or an array) makes `replaceAll` throw a TypeError that is not caught, producing an unhandled 500 instead of a 400. Similarly `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` at line 58 throws if the stored blob cannot be decrypted/parsed. Validate the body (zod/typeof check) and wrap the decrypt/parse in a try/catch returning a proper error code.

findings.title: Backup codes are stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed
findings.body: `backupCodes` is persisted as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`, so anyone who obtains a database dump plus the (usually env-deployed, long-lived) `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` recovers every user's usable recovery credentials in plaintext. Unlike `twoFactorSecret`, backup codes never need to be displayed again after setup — only compared — so they should be stored as one-way hashes (e.g. per-code hash, compared by hashing the submitted code) to limit the impact of a DB/key compromise.

findings.title: resetState() leaves backup codes in memory and leaks the blob URL
findings.body: `resetState()` clears only `password`, `errorMessage` and `step`; `backupCodes`, `backupCodesUrl`, `dataUri` and `secret` persist. The `URL.createObjectURL` blob is only revoked on the next successful `handleSetup` call, so closing the dialog (or navigating away) leaks the object URL for the page's lifetime, and the plaintext recovery codes stay in component state after the dialog is closed. Revoke the URL and clear the code state in `resetState()`/on unmount.

findings.title: Assertion is a no-op and the new backup-code auth paths are untested
findings.body: `expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts on the returned Promise, which is always truthy, so this step passes even when 2FA was not enabled — the PR adds a FIXME comment acknowledging this but leaves the broken assertion in place (use `await expect(locator).toBeChecked()` or the `data-state="checked"` selector as the second test does). In addition, the only new coverage is clicking download/copy/close on the backup-code screen; the actual security-relevant paths added by this PR — logging in with a backup code, single-use invalidation of a redeemed code, and disabling 2FA with a backup code — have no tests at all (only a TODO), which is how issues like the password-bypass and case-sensitivity problems go unnoticed.
